titre: Thorndike's Puzzle Box, and the Curve That Contradicts Intuition
accroche: A hungry cat, locked in a crate, eventually works a latch to get out and eat. The intelligence we see in it is not the one we think.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1898, Edward Thorndike, a doctoral student at Columbia under James McKeen Cattell, locks hungry cats in crates about fifty centimeters by forty, and thirty high. A latch, operated by a pedal, a button, or a loop of string, opens the door and gives access to food placed outside. At first the cat struggles, squeezes between the bars, meows, scratches. After a few minutes, sometimes more, it works the mechanism by chance and gets out.

## A Curve, Not a Flash

Thorndike repeats the trial dozens of times with the same animal and times each escape. Plotted on a graph, the escape times of six kittens draw a slope that descends gradually, with no sharp break. This is the point he is trying to settle: a cat that suddenly understood the mechanism would see its time collapse all at once; a cat learning by trial and error would, on the contrary, show slow improvement, as useless movements fade and the right gesture is reinforced. “The change is as a fact very gradual,” writes Thorndike. None of the animals shows a break.

Thorndike pushes the test further with a verbal discrimination task, in which the cat must respond differently depending on the sentence spoken in front of it. It takes sixty trials for it to react reliably to “I must feed those cats,” and three hundred eighty trials to discriminate perfectly the opposite sentence, “I will not feed them.” Showing the animal what to do, or physically guiding its paw to the right button, speeds up nothing: learning does not come through imitation or demonstration, but through the repetition of a movement followed by a reward.

## What This Shifts

Thorndike draws a conclusion that goes beyond cats: he finds in them no trace of inference, comparison, or reasoning. What the common sense of the time describes as animal intelligence, a cat that “understands” how to get out, turns out to be a more modest mechanism: gestures followed by satisfaction are repeated, the others fade. This law of effect will become one of the pillars of nascent behaviorism. Thorndike himself will correct part of it three decades later, in 1929, acknowledging that punishment proves not as effective as he had first supposed for erasing an association. What has held up since is the image of the gradual curve, set against the flash of understanding too readily credited to an animal that merely got lucky at the right moment.

carte.punch: A cat that escapes from a crate has not “understood” how to do it.
carte.idee: In 1898, Thorndike locks hungry cats in latched crates. Their escape times, repeated, draw a curve that descends little by little, never a sudden drop. For Thorndike, it is proof of learning by trial and error, not by reasoning.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Traces the law of effect through to its behaviorist and connectionist critics.

quiz.question: Why does the learning curve of Thorndike's cats count against the idea of an intelligence that “understands” the puzzle box?
choix: Because escape times decrease gradually, with no sudden drop that would signal a flash of understanding
Because no cat ever managed to escape from the crate in under ten minutes
Because Thorndike tested only one cat, which makes any generalization impossible
Because the cats showed improvement only after watching another cat escape
quiz.explication: A sudden understanding of the mechanism would produce a sharp drop in escape time. Thorndike observes the opposite in the six kittens he follows: a gradual slope, with no break, a sign of learning by trial and error. Watching another cat succeed speeds up nothing, contrary to what the last choice says.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In Thorndike's verbal discrimination task, how many trials does the cat need to discriminate perfectly the opposite sentence, “I will not feed them”?
choix: Sixty trials, as for the first sentence
A single trial, once the mechanism has been shown
Six trials, as many as the kittens tested
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It takes sixty trials to react reliably to the first sentence, but three hundred eighty trials to discriminate perfectly the opposite sentence: learning remains gradual.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Thorndike, what effect does showing the cat what to do, or physically guiding its paw to the right button, have on its learning?
choix: It clearly speeds up learning, which then becomes nearly immediate
It speeds up nothing, as learning does not come through imitation or demonstration
It slows down learning, as the cat distrusts the imposed gesture
It changes nothing for the kittens but clearly speeds up learning in adult cats
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Thorndike finds that showing the gesture or guiding the paw speeds up nothing: learning comes through the repetition of a movement followed by a reward, not through imitation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Thorndike revise in 1929 about his law of effect, formulated in 1898?
choix: He abandoned the whole idea of learning by trial and error
He concluded that cats reason far more than he had thought in 1898
He replaced his cats with rats in all his later experiments
He acknowledged that punishment erases an association less well than he had thought
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Three decades later, Thorndike acknowledges that punishment proves not as effective as he had first supposed for erasing an association, without abandoning learning by trial and error.
